title: Sustainability standards and certification

definition.text: Voluntary guidelines that producers, traders and retailers follow to show they use good environmental, social, ethical and food-safety practices.

facts.text: More than 400 such standards exist around the world.
A standard is usually written by stakeholders and experts in a sector and lists practices, such as how a crop should be grown sustainably.
Certification checks that a business meets the standard, and traceability follows certified goods along the supply chain, often ending in a label for shoppers.
The standards grew up where national and global laws were weak but consumers and campaign groups demanded action.
Some standards set a high bar and work with top performers, while others aim to remove the worst practices across most of an industry.
Standards also differ in whether checking is done by a first, second or third party and whether certified and uncertified material may be mixed.
Agriculture has the most widely adopted standards: 40% of global coffee production is certified, and about 15–20% of cocoa and tea production meets major standards.
Researchers continue to debate how effective these schemes are and how they are governed.

contested_note: Academic work examines both the benefits of individual certification schemes and continuing disputes over their effectiveness and governance.

title: Voluntary consensus versus private standards
article: Sustainability standards and certification#International and private standards supporting sustainability

definition.text: Sustainability standards fall into two groups: voluntary consensus standards and private standards.

facts.text: The International Organization for Standardization develops sustainability standards through a voluntary consensus process.
Individual companies created private standards of their own, such as Starbucks' C.A.F.E. Practices and Nespresso AAA.
Some standards were launched by coalitions of firms, NGOs and development agencies to harmonize rules, such as the Marine Stewardship Council standard.

definition.text: A labelling system on food and consumer products that tells shoppers about the product's environmental impact.

facts.text: Ecolabels are voluntary, whereas green stickers are required by law.
There are 456 ecolabels in 199 countries across 25 industry sectors, according to the Ecolabel Index.
Some labels measure pollution or energy use with scores or units, while others certify that a set of minimum practices was followed.
Through certification, a farm, forest, fishery or mine can show it meets a standard and sell its products as certified.
Some manufacturers have set up 'rubber stamp' labels to greenwash products, so trust in labels is an issue for consumers.
The German Blue Angel, from 1978, was the world's first ecolabel.
Labels apply market pressure on industries to cut their environmental impact by linking products to informed consumer wishes.

definition.text: The International Organization for Standardization sorts environmental labels into three types by what they cover and how strictly they are checked.

facts.text: Type I (ISO 14024) is a voluntary multi-criteria label checked by an independent third party that looks at a product's life cycle impacts.
Type II (ISO 14021) is a claim a manufacturer or retailer makes about itself without third-party auditing.
Type III (ISO/TR 14025) is a declaration of measured life cycle data that does not rate the product but helps buyers compare.
'Type I-like' labels cover a single issue, such as a pass/fail energy limit for appliances.

definition.text: The concern that the spread of ecolabels creates obstacles to international trade other than tariffs.

facts.text: To qualify for a foreign ecolabel, exporters must adjust to each market's production standards, which can cost money, information and expertise.
Labelling programs often reflect the importing country's priorities and technologies and may not fit the exporting country's environment.
Since 1995 the World Trade Organization agreements have covered the possible effects of voluntary product standards and labels.

definition.text: The idea that ecolabelling is a self-regulating, market-based policy tool that partly takes over from government command and control.

facts.text: Eco-labelling standards are voluntary but put market pressure on large companies to adopt greener production.
Ecolabelling has become a form of non-state authority at national and international levels.
At the 1992 Earth Summit, countries agreed to bring environmental issues into manufacturing and to steer consumption toward sustainable development.

definition.text: A repeating process in which consumers, firms, governments and institutions interact through ecolabels to produce eco-innovation.

facts.text: Ecolabelling encourages new green products and improves firms' environmental management strategy.
In the cycle, consumers' expectations are met, firms gain value, and governments foster cleaner production and consumption.

definition.text: Labels on consumer appliances that show whether they use energy efficiently compared with similar products.

facts.text: The yellow US EnergyGuide label estimates an appliance's energy use, compares it with similar products and lists rough yearly running costs.
Canadian law requires the EnerGuide label on every new electrical appliance made in or imported into Canada.
These labels show energy used in operation, while energy input labelling shows the energy used to make the product.

definition.text: A government measure that keeps energy prices below market levels for customers, keeps them above market levels for suppliers, or cuts their costs.

facts.text: Energy subsidies can be direct cash payments or indirect support such as tax exemptions, price controls, trade restrictions and limits on market access.
The International Renewable Energy Agency tracked some $634 billion in energy subsidies in 2020, around 70% of them for fossil fuels.
Of that 2020 total, about 20% went to renewable power, 6% to biofuels and just over 3% to nuclear.
Other forms include public research, cheap government services, demand guarantees, and failing to charge for external costs such as pollution.
Choosing to subsidize one energy source more than another can affect the environment.
Early support for solar power by the United States and Germany helped bring renewable energy to market and cut emissions worldwide.
Because energy policies are interconnected across countries, regulating subsidies at the World Trade Organization is often seen as necessary.

title: Arguments for and against energy subsidies
article: Energy subsidy#Overview of all sources of energy

definition.text: The debate over whether governments should support energy prices or producers, weighing supply security and social aims against waste and environmental harm.

facts.text: Supporters say subsidies secure domestic supply, cut air pollution, help meet climate pledges, widen access to energy for the poor and protect jobs.
Critics say fossil fuel subsidies raise consumption and waste, burden public finances and hold back cleaner technologies.
In developing countries most benefits of fossil fuel subsidies go to the richest 20% of households.
The World Bank found subsidies to large energy companies unjustified but saw a case for helping the poorest households get modern energy.

contested_note: Sources set out explicit arguments for and against energy subsidies, and reform is opposed by many who see it as governments taking something away.

definition.text: A policy that makes manufacturers responsible for the environmental costs of their products across the whole life cycle, mainly the costs of dealing with them as waste.

facts.text: The concept was first formally put forward in Sweden by Thomas Lindhqvist in a 1990 report to the Swedish environment ministry.
It uses money incentives: producers who pay end-of-life costs are pushed to design greener products.
It rests on the idea that brand owners control product design and so are best placed to cut toxicity and waste.
It can take the form of reuse, buyback or recycling programs, and producers may pay a producer responsibility organization to handle used products.
Unlike product stewardship, which shares responsibility along the chain, it puts the cost of recycling into the product price and relieves local governments.
In Germany, packaging use per person fell from 94.7 kg to 82 kg between 1991 and 1998 after EPR was adopted, a reduction of 13.4%.
A drawback is the administrative burden from rules that differ between countries and waste streams.
The deposit-refund system is described as based on the principles of extended producer responsibility.

definition.text: Waste policies that require manufacturers to take back their products at the end of their useful life, or to help pay for collection and recycling.

facts.text: They were adopted where collection of hazardous products was lacking or too costly for local governments.
They aim to encourage designs for reuse and recycling, put waste costs into product prices and promote recycling innovation.
The earliest take-back schemes began in Europe, driven by scarce landfill space and hazardous parts.

title: Extended producer responsibility for electronics

definition.text: The use of producer responsibility rules to deal with e-waste, used electronic equipment that cannot safely go out with household trash.

facts.text: E-waste contains lead, mercury, brominated flame-retardants and cadmium, which are dangerous to health and the environment.
Making producers pay for recycling may lead them to design less toxic, longer-lasting electronics, so EPR is cited as a tool against planned obsolescence.
Critics worry it could raise prices, slow innovation, or let manufacturers shred second-hand goods instead of reusing them.

contested_note: Supporters say it drives greener design while critics argue it raises costs, slows innovation and is not clearly speeding greener design.

title: Fossil fuel subsidies

definition.text: Energy subsidies for coal, oil and gas: any government action that lowers the cost of producing fossil fuel energy, raises producers' prices or lowers consumers' prices.

facts.text: Under a narrow definition they totalled around $725 billion (0.6% of global GDP) to $900 billion in 2024; under a broader one, $6.7 trillion (5.8% of GDP).
Most of the money supports oil and natural gas.
They are mainly consumption subsidies, such as lower sales tax on home-heating gas, or production subsidies, such as tax breaks for oil exploration.
Letting fuel users pollute the air and warm the climate without paying is also counted as a subsidy under broad definitions.
They act as a negative carbon price and use government money that could be spent on other things.
Economists agree the rich get most of the absolute benefit, since the poorest people usually do not own cars.
Subsidies are estimated to cause hundreds of thousands of deaths from air pollution each year.
Removing them would cut air-pollution health risks and greatly reduce global carbon emissions.

notes: Totals differ because the IMF counts unpriced externalities and the OECD/IEA do not (S:d03b49975cdc); treated as definitional, not conflicts.

title: Measuring fossil fuel subsidies

definition.text: Ways of estimating fossil fuel subsidies by adding up government payments, comparing domestic prices with world prices, and sometimes counting health and climate damage.

facts.text: Counting unpriced externalities makes IMF estimates far larger than those using the OECD and International Energy Agency definitions.
In 2021 the UK government said it did not subsidize fossil fuels under the IEA definition, while others said it did under the OECD definition.
An IMF paper found underpricing of local air pollution was the largest part of global subsidies at 42%, followed by global warming costs at 29%.
The fiscal cost of government support for fossil fuels was 1.1 trillion USD in 2023, 90% of it tied to consumption.

contested_note: Governments and analysts dispute which definition to use, and so whether some countries subsidize fossil fuels at all.

title: Nudge theory

definition.text: The idea from behavioural science that changing how choices are presented (choice architecture) can steer people's behaviour without forcing them.

facts.text: Nudging differs from other ways of getting compliance, such as education, legislation or enforcement.
The 2008 book Nudge by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein made the idea popular.
A nudge alters the setting so that fast, automatic thinking favours the desired choice.
Nudges are small, cheap changes; techniques include defaults, social proof and making an option more noticeable.
More consumers chose renewable electricity when it was offered as the default option.
In tourism, nudges led people to reuse towels, choose more sustainable hotels and offset their carbon voluntarily.
Governments use them through 'nudge units', such as the British Behavioural Insights Team set up in 2010.
A 2021 meta-analysis found nudging effective with moderate publication bias, but a later correction for that bias found no evidence of an effect.

contested_note: The effectiveness of nudges is disputed: meta-analyses disagree once publication bias is corrected, and critics question their ethics and lasting effect.

title: Precautionary principle

definition.text: An approach to new activities or technologies that might cause harm when scientific knowledge about them is still incomplete, favouring caution and review first.

facts.text: Policy makers often use it when a decision might cause harm and conclusive evidence is not yet available.
The English term is generally thought to come from the German Vorsorgeprinzip, adopted in the 1970s in response to forest decline and sea pollution.
It shifts the burden of proof: whoever proposes an activity must show it will not, or is very unlikely to, cause significant harm.
Its second core idea is that the response should be proportionate to the risk and to the cost and feasibility of acting.
One study found 14 different formulations of the principle in treaties and declarations.
EU environmental policy must be based on the precautionary principle along with prevention, fixing damage at source and polluter pays.
It is typically applied to climate change, new organisms such as GMOs, public health threats and long-term effects of new technologies.
Critics argue it is vague, self-cancelling, unscientific and an obstacle to progress.

contested_note: Supporters see it as needed caution under uncertainty, while critics call it vague, incoherent and a barrier to innovation.

definition.text: Two versions of the precautionary principle: the strong one requires regulation whenever harm is possible, the weak one only permits action without full proof.

facts.text: Strong precaution demands regulation even if the evidence is speculative and the economic costs are high, a 'no-regrets' stance that ignores cost.
The 1982 UN World Charter for Nature gave the first international recognition to the strong version.
Weak formulations allow benefits to be weighed against costs, and economic factors may justify delay.
People practise weak precaution daily, such as buying smoke detectors or wearing seatbelts.

title: Precautionary approach (Rio Principle 15)

definition.text: A softer form of the precautionary principle, set out in Principle 15 of the 1992 Rio Declaration, that takes local capabilities and costs into account.

facts.text: Principle 15 says that where serious or irreversible damage threatens, lack of full scientific certainty is no reason to postpone cost-effective preventive measures.
The United States has opposed the word 'principle' in negotiations because a principle of law is a source of law.
The Cartagena Protocol on Biosafety builds on the precautionary approach of Principle 15.

contested_note: The line between the precautionary principle and the precautionary approach is described as diffuse and sometimes controversial.

title: Precautionary dilemma

definition.text: The common objection that weak versions of the precautionary principle are trivial and strong versions are incoherent.

facts.text: Cass Sunstein argued that the weak version only states a truism.
Applying strong precaution can itself cause harm by blocking innovation and keeping current harmful technologies in use.
For example, banning nuclear plants over low-probability risks means continued reliance on fossil-fuel plants and their air-pollution deaths.

contested_note: Critics hold that no version of the principle is both useful and coherent, a view its defenders reject.

definition.text: A form of government spending that passes money from taxpayers to individuals, households or businesses to support them or encourage some activity.

facts.text: Subsidies take forms such as direct spending, tax incentives, cheap loans, price support and government-provided goods and services.
The word can also cover support from NGOs or international organizations, not only governments.
Governments may hand out direct payments in a downturn to help people pay bills and to boost economic activity.
Spending on subsidies stays high in many countries, often several percentage points of GDP.
Some governments subsidise rail and bus transport, which cut congestion and pollution compared with cars.
Many subsidies create perverse incentives and harmful unintended consequences.

definition.text: Subsidies are sorted as direct or indirect, production or consumption, and broad or narrow.

facts.text: Direct subsidies are cash outlays to a specific person or household, such as cash grants; indirect ones include tax breaks and low-interest loans.
Production subsidies help suppliers expand output by offsetting costs; consumption subsidies lower the price consumers pay.
Consumption subsidies are most common in developing countries, for basics such as food, water, electricity and education.
Broad subsidies are hard to identify and include non-monetary support; environmental externalities are the most common type.

definition.text: How a subsidy changes a market: it shifts the supply or demand curve to the right by the amount of the subsidy.

facts.text: In a competitive market, a subsidy pushes supply beyond the equilibrium quantity, creating deadweight loss.
Deadweight loss from a subsidy is the amount by which its cost exceeds its gains, and it grows with the subsidy's size.
A demand subsidy tends to raise prices, while a supply subsidy can lower them.
Subsidized goods sold abroad lower world prices, hurting producers in poorer countries and causing trade tensions.
In 2019 the OECD urged countries to use more environmental taxation and phase out agricultural subsidies and environmentally harmful tax breaks.

definition.text: Subsidies whose effects are clearly and significantly harmful both to the economy and to the environment.

facts.text: A subsidy rarely starts out perverse but can become so if it is not withdrawn after reaching its goal.
They drain government budgets away from priorities such as conservation, education and health.
They cause environmental damage such as resource overuse and pollution, and tend to benefit the rich at the expense of the poor.
They become 'locked' into society through bureaucratic roadblocks and institutional inertia, so they are hard to remove.
In 2005 US farmers received $14 billion and EU farmers $47 billion in agricultural subsidies.
Government subsidies in agriculture often fuel environmental damage, deforestation and overfishing.

definition.text: Government support for fishing, such as direct aid to fishers, loans, tax breaks, infrastructure and price support.

facts.text: In 2002 the WWF estimated that about 75% of the world's major fisheries were overexploited.
These subsidies expand fleets and catches, favouring large-scale operations over small-scale fishers.
Together they keep marine fisheries overcapitalized and overfished.

title: Carbon emission label

definition.text: A label stating the carbon dioxide emitted in making, transporting or disposing of a consumer product.

facts.text: The first carbon label, the Carbon Reduction Label, was introduced in the UK in 2006 by the Carbon Trust.
The Carbon Trust label required companies to commit to cutting the product's embodied carbon or lose the label.
The Swiss climatop label instead marks products at least 20% better than others in their category.
Carbon labels focus on greenhouse gas emissions rather than direct energy use.

notes: Page is a seed of another chapter; drafted here because the footprint chapter cites it twice. Fold or drop at merge if that chapter has it.

title: Forest certification

definition.text: A voluntary system that certifies wood and paper products as coming from forests managed responsibly under a particular standard.

facts.text: An independent body writes the forest management standard, and independent auditors certify forest operations that meet it.
Credible programs protect biodiversity and water quality, keep harvests sustainable and require prompt replanting.
Third-party forest certification was pioneered in the early 1990s by the Forest Stewardship Council (FSC), a collaboration of environmental groups, forest companies and social interests.
With no single international standard, more than 50 scheme owners offer forest certification worldwide.
The two largest international programs are the FSC and the PEFC, and PEFC covers about two-thirds of certified forest area.
About 10% of the world's forest is under at least one certification program.
Some commentators, including Jared Diamond, say logging companies set up rival standards to confuse consumers.
Demand is driven by publishers' paper commitments, green public procurement, green building standards and laws against illegal logging.

contested_note: Critics such as Greenpeace and Jared Diamond question the rigour of competing private forest standards, which the schemes defend.

definition.text: Certification that tracks certified material through every stage of processing and distribution, from the forest to the consumer.

facts.text: It provides evidence that certified material in a product really comes from certified forests.
It keeps certified material identified or separate from non-certified material during manufacture.
Between January 2009 and May 2010, PEFC and FSC chain-of-custody certificates rose 88% to 23,717 worldwide.

title: Common Agricultural Policy

definition.text: The European Union's farm policy, which runs a system of agricultural subsidies, risk management tools and other programmes.

facts.text: It was introduced in 1962 and has been changed to cut its share of the budget, from 73% in 1985 to 37% in 2017, and to add rural development.
The 'Agenda 2000' reforms split it into two pillars: production support and rural development.
Critics say it creates artificially high food prices, helped by import tariffs estimated at 18–28%.
Guaranteed prices led the EU to buy and store huge surpluses, nicknamed 'butter mountains' and 'wine lakes'.
Because it has rewarded higher output, larger farms have gained far more from subsidies than smaller ones.
A 2024 study reported that 80% of its subsidies in 2013 supported emissions-intensive animal products.

contested_note: The policy has been criticised by many interests since its start, and even the European Commission acknowledges its defects.

title: Decoupling and cross compliance
article: Common Agricultural Policy#European Commission Report and decoupling (2003)

definition.text: The 2003 reform of EU farm support that cut the link between subsidies and particular crops and tied payments to environmental and other conditions.

facts.text: Farmers who fail the strict environmental requirements of cross compliance face cuts in their subsidies.
The aim was to free more money for environmental quality and animal welfare programmes.
In England the Single Payment Scheme paid a flat rate of around £230 per hectare for keeping land fit for cultivation.

distinct_from: Environmental effects of the Common Agricultural Policy

title: Environmental effects of the Common Agricultural Policy

definition.text: The criticism that EU farm subsidies drove a large expansion of production using fertilisers and pesticides, with serious environmental harm.

facts.text: Between 1980 and 2009 the farmland bird population fell from 600 million to 300 million, a loss of 50%.
Removing hedgerows and ploughing meadows made farming more efficient but cut farmland bird habitat.
In 2010 the EU said 31% of €5 billion for new agricultural challenges would go to protecting biodiversity in the countryside.
In 2024 the European Court of Auditors warned the policy was not aligned with the EU's Green Deal climate goals.

contested_note: Critics blame the policy for environmental damage, while reforms since 2004 claim to put the environment at the centre of farm policy.

title: CAP rural development pillar
article: Common Agricultural Policy#Rural development policy (structural policy, Pillar II)

definition.text: The second pillar of the EU farm policy, in effect since 2000, which funds the economic, social and environmental development of the countryside.

facts.text: One of its three axes supports land management that improves the environment and helps fight climate change.
Projects can include protecting water quality, sustainable land management and planting trees against erosion and floods.
It works through seven-year rural development programmes, of which there are 118 in the EU.

distinct_from: Environmental effects of the Common Agricultural Policy

definition.text: A voluntary energy-efficiency labelling program set up by the US Environmental Protection Agency in 1992.

facts.text: It began as a voluntary label for computers and displays and now covers more than 75 product categories plus homes, commercial buildings and industrial plants.
Before 2011 products qualified on manufacturers' own data, which auditors found open to fraud; since then independent labs and certifiers must test them.
Supporters cited estimated yearly energy cost savings of more than $40 billion against about $32 million in yearly EPA funding.
An Energy Star label shows a product beats minimum guidelines, but it is not always the most efficient option available.

definition.text: A voluntary form of environmental regulation in which a company chooses to meet processes or goals set by a certification service.

facts.text: Most certification services have a logo, commonly called an ecolabel, that certified products can carry.
It is seen as a form of corporate social responsibility, letting firms reduce environmental harm by following external, measured objectives.
Companies take it up to sell ethical products, improve their image, get on better with stakeholders and earn more profit.
It only works if there are consumers willing to buy the resulting green products.
Consumers may be willing to pay extra for ethically produced goods.
Firms may seek certification to avoid accusations of greenwashing by having their green claims checked independently.

definition.text: The drawbacks of voluntary environmental certification, including high costs, weak incentives for poor performers and gaps in what it covers.

facts.text: Usually only the best-performing operators get certified, so firms with no interest in environmental management stay outside.
Suppliers usually bear the costs, and the extra profit often does not cover them.
Many certification costs are fixed, so large producers gain an advantage over small ones through economies of scale.
Tropical deforestation usually comes from converting forest to other uses, which lies outside forest management certification.

title: Eco-Management and Audit Scheme

definition.text: A standard for environmental management systems, developed by the European Commission in 1993, that helps organisations assess, manage and keep improving their environmental performance.

facts.text: It is the EU's voluntary environmental management instrument and is open to any type of organisation worldwide.
Registering involves an environmental review, policy, programme, management system, internal audit and a public environmental statement.
Only accredited independent verifiers supervised by government bodies may validate the environmental statements.
Since 2010 registered organisations must report indicators on energy, materials, water, waste, biodiversity and emissions.

notes: Registration counts differ: 4,600 organisations / 7,900 sites (S:9d30045373e3) vs 4,400 / 8,150 (S:c0af58158e55); both say 'currently', probably different dates.

definition.text: A trade arrangement meant to help producers in developing countries get sustainable and fair conditions, by paying higher prices and raising social and environmental standards.

facts.text: It focuses on commodities exported from poorer to richer countries, notably handicrafts, coffee, cocoa, wine, sugar, fruit, flowers and gold.
The current movement took shape in Europe in the 1960s, and sales only took off once Fairtrade certification labels arrived.
Fairtrade labelling uses independent audits of producers and traders, and the guarantee of a minimum price is its most distinctive feature.
In 2011 more than 1.2 million farmers and workers in over 60 countries took part in Fairtrade International's system.
Coffee is the most established fair trade commodity.
Direct trade, which skips certification overhead, is proposed as an alternative.

definition.text: Extra money that buyers of fair trade goods pay to producer groups, who decide democratically how to spend it.

facts.text: Under Fairtrade the premium goes to the cooperative rather than directly to individual producers.
Groups often spend it on public goods that government fails to provide, such as environmental projects, schools and water projects.
In 2011 Fairtrade International's system paid €65 million in premiums to producers for community development.

title: Criticism of fair trade

definition.text: The debate over whether fair trade actually benefits poor producers, given studies that find both gains and little effect.

facts.text: A 2015 study found producer benefits close to zero because of an oversupply of certification.
Little of the extra retail price may reach farmers: one estimate found US exporters received only 2% of a US$5 per pound retail premium on coffee.
Because coffee demand is highly inelastic, economists argue higher fair trade output can push down prices for the many non-certified farmers.
A study in the Journal of Economic Perspectives found it meets many of its goals, though on a modest scale.

contested_note: Studies disagree on whether fair trade raises producers' incomes and working conditions or mostly benefits intermediaries.

definition.text: A policy that speeds up investment in renewable energy by giving producers long-term contracts at a guaranteed, usually above-market price for the electricity they supply.

facts.text: Feed-in tariffs usually guarantee grid access, offer long-term contracts and pay prices based on generating costs.
Contracts typically run 15–25 years, and the price often falls over time to follow and encourage technology cost cuts.
Different technologies get different prices; wind and solar PV, for example, get more per kWh than tidal power.
A 2008 European Commission analysis found well-designed feed-in tariffs the most efficient and effective support for renewable electricity.
When funded by a surcharge on bills they raise power prices, adding 6.88 cents/kWh for German households in 2017.
Renewables can also lower spot market prices through the merit order effect, which happened in Spain, Denmark and Germany.
As of 2019 more than 50 countries had feed-in tariff policies.

definition.text: The point at which electricity from an alternative technology costs the same as the average grid electricity price in an area.

facts.text: Parity can vary over the day, over years and from place to place.
In some areas wind, landfill gas and biomass power are already cheaper than grid electricity.
Parity has been reached in areas that use feed-in tariffs.

definition.text: Government strategy to speed the growth of green industries, correcting market failures and moving toward a low-carbon economy.

facts.text: Green industries such as renewable energy face high costs and risks, so they need public support until they become commercially viable.
Subsidies for a targeted sector are its most common form; tools also include R&D funding, tax credits, feed-in tariffs, mandates and green public procurement.
New sustainable technologies cannot compete at once with existing ones because of path dependency, so governments nurture technological niches.
German green industrial policy helped build a renewable energy industry employing over 371,000 people, double the jobs of 2004.
Without government intervention the market is unlikely to move to a low-carbon economy on its own.

title: Risks of green industrial policy

definition.text: The concerns that governments may back the wrong firms or industries and that support invites rent-seeking and regulatory capture.

facts.text: Subsidies are especially prone to rent-seeking, because special interests lobby to keep them even when they are no longer needed.
Policy may end up driven by political rather than economic concerns.
Some failures are inevitable, and governments can reduce risk by testing policies in parts of the country first.

contested_note: Proponents and sceptics agree there are risks but disagree on whether governments can pick industries well enough to justify the policy.

definition.text: Rules requiring producers to source a minimum share of goods, labour or services locally.

facts.text: Ontario's 2009 Green Energy and Green Economy Act made wind and solar farms use Ontario-made parts to qualify for subsidies.
The Ontario law created many jobs, cut emissions and greatly expanded the province's renewable energy industry.

definition.text: A set of international standards for environmental management systems, first issued by the International Organization for Standardization in 1996.

facts.text: The standards help organizations cut their harm to air, water and land, comply with laws, and keep improving.
Like ISO 9000, they concern how a product or service is made rather than the product itself.
ISO 14001 is the core standard; it sets out a framework for an environmental management system but no required level of environmental performance.
The series is voluntary, and certification is done by third parties rather than by ISO itself.
As of 2017, there were more than 300,000 ISO 14001 certifications in 171 countries.
Firms adopting it can cut waste, resource use and operating costs and may gain a competitive advantage.
Its predecessor was BS 7750, the world's first environmental management system standard, published in 1992.

definition.text: The four-step management cycle of Plan, Do, Check and Act on which ISO 14001 environmental management is based.

facts.text: Planning starts with a review of how the organization's operations interact with the environment, its 'environmental aspects'.
In the Check stage, performance is measured against targets and internal audits are held.
A management review then resets targets, feeding a process of continual improvement.

title: Inflation Reduction Act

definition.text: A 2022 United States law that is the largest federal legislation ever to address climate change, mainly through tax credits and grants for clean energy.

facts.text: According to the CBO and JCT it invests $783 billion in energy security and climate provisions.
It gives consumers 10 years of tax credits for heat pumps, rooftop solar and efficient electric heating and cooling.
It created a $27 billion green bank, the Greenhouse Gas Reduction Fund, to finance smaller regional green banks.
Rhodium Group raised its forecast of 2030 US emission cuts from 17–30% to 29–42% below 2005 levels after the act.

notes: Single-country law kept as the main worked example of green subsidies through tax credits; coordinator may set exclude under the country-law rule. Climate spending estimates differ: $783 billion (CBO/JCT, S:c073ac45c1fa) vs around $375 billion over 10 years (S:6b6cd129a1fd); scope likely differs.

definition.text: A system that collects and publishes information on releases and transfers of hazardous substances from industrial and other facilities.

facts.text: Several countries set them up after the 1984 Bhopal disaster and the 1992 Rio conference, which affirmed people's right to know about toxic chemicals.
They aim to give nearby residents the same information as companies, since a level playing field matters for acceptance of permit decisions.
A protocol to the Aarhus Convention requires its parties to set up such registers; the 2003 Kyiv Protocol was the first binding international instrument on them.
Data come mainly from facility questionnaires and remain the facilities' own estimates, even after official checks.

definition.text: A public US database of toxic chemical releases and waste management activities reported by industrial and federal facilities.

facts.text: Congress created it in 1986 under the Emergency Planning and Community Right-to-Know Act, prompted by the 1984 Bhopal disaster.
For most listed chemicals, facilities must report if they make 25,000 pounds or process or use 10,000 pounds a year.
Facilities report releases to air, water and land and amounts of waste sent off-site.

definition.text: Buying goods, services and works in a way that gives value for money over the whole life cycle while also benefiting society and staying within the environment's limits.

facts.text: Procurement has traditionally weighed only price and quality; sustainable procurement adds the third-party effects of buying decisions.
It favours renewable or recycled materials and less waste, and checks suppliers for pollution or harm to habitats.
Public spending averages 12% of GDP in OECD countries and up to 30% in developing countries, giving governments enormous purchasing power.
Purchases can exceed 50% of a company's expenses, and over 80% in retail, electronics and cars, so firms can also shift markets.
Sustainable options often cost about the same, and even pricier ones can save money through lower energy, water and waste costs over their life.

definition.text: The part of sustainable public procurement that uses government buying power to reach environmental goals.

facts.text: It aims to cut greenhouse gas emissions, improve resource efficiency and grow the market for greener products.
It relies heavily on life cycle costing, which counts transport, installation, training, insurance and running costs as well as the purchase price.
Rules steer public bodies to buy items such as efficient computers, recycled paper, electric vehicles and renewable energy, which can drive green innovation.

title: Sustainable seafood advisory lists and certification
article: Sustainable seafood advisory lists and certification

definition.text: Guides and certification schemes meant to make seafood supply chains transparent and help shoppers choose seafood from well-managed stocks.

facts.text: Their economic impact is unclear, but they bring non-monetary gains such as better reputation and reorganised supply chains.
The Marine Stewardship Council runs a certification program for consumer seafood products.
Many conservationists feel the growing number of seafood labels is confusing consumers.

definition.text: Part of a government's tax policy that encourages a particular economic activity by lowering the tax owed.

facts.text: For individuals they include deductions, exemptions and credits, such as the hybrid vehicle tax credit.
Tax incentives aimed at single companies are generally seen as inefficient, costly, distorting and regressive.
A 2020 study found some job gains from US state and local business incentives but no evidence of wider economic growth.
Badly designed incentives can harm a government's finances.
Conservation projects have traditionally drawn on public money that includes tax incentives.

title: Voluntary environmental agreements

definition.text: Policy tools in which firms or other actors agree, without being forced, to take environmental action, often in a deal with government.

facts.text: They differ from market-based instruments and from command-and-control rules, where authorities dictate the performance or technology required.
Since the 1980s many governments have turned from regulation toward 'new' instruments, notably market instruments and voluntary agreements.
In industrial countries they let companies gain recognition for going beyond minimum regulatory standards.
In developing countries such as in Latin America, they are more often used to fix widespread non-compliance with mandatory rules.
The EU first tackled car CO2 emissions through a voluntary agreement and later replaced it with mandatory limits for new cars.
